source_text: δ' ἐπάγεσθαι τἀγαθὰ πάντα παριστῶν τὴν μίαν θεϊκὴν εἰρήνην, ἧς «ὅριον οὐκ ἔστιν», περὶ ἧς Ἠσαΐας διακέκραγεν· «κύριε ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν, εἰρήνην δὸς ἡμῖν· πάντα γὰρ ἀπέδωκας ἡμῖν. κύριε, ἐκτὸς σοῦ ἄλλον οὐκ οἴδαμεν», ὡς αὐτοῦ τυγχάνουσαν διὰ τὸ ἐπίκοινον τῆς φύσεως καὶ κυριότητος δίδωσιν κατ' ἐξουσίαν. 26.3 ἔφη γάρ· «εἰρήνην ἀφίημι ὑμῖν, εἰρήνην τὴν ἐμὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν». 26.4 ∆ιὸ οὐχ ἥκιστα καὶ Παῦλος τοῦτο τὸ θεόσδοτον χρῆμα ἄμφω τὰς ἀγενήτους ὑποστάσεις ἀπαραλλάκτως χορηγεῖν ἔφη, 26.5 Ῥωμαίοις οὕτω που γράψας· «χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ». 26.6 διάγνωσιν δὲ ἡμῖν τοῦτ' αὐτὸ οὕτως ἔχειν παρέσχετο καὶ τό· «πάντα ὅσα ἔχει ὁ πατὴρ ἐμά ἐστιν». 26.7 ταῦτα γὰρ οὐκ ἀμαθῶς εἰς τὴν κτίσιν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὴν θεϊκὴν ἀξίαν ἐκλαμβάνεται, εἰ ἀξίαν ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ φάναι χρή. 26.8 Θεὸς γάρ, φησίν, ἐστὶν ὁ πατήρ. εἰμὶ καὶ ἐγώ· υἱὸς γὰρ αὐτοῦ μονογενὴς καὶ ἀληθινὸς καὶ ἀγαπητός. 26.9 Κύριός ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ. εἰμὶ καὶ ἐγὼ πάντων κύριος καὶ κληρονόμος ζῶντος πατρὸς τῆς κληρονομίας δεσπόζων. 26.10 κληρονομῶ δὲ τὰ ἑαυτοῦ, τοῦτο μὲν ὡς ποιητὴς αὐτῶν, τοῦτο δὲ καὶ ὡς γνήσιος υἱός. 26.11 ἐτέθην δὲ κληρονόμος ὡς ἐνανθρωπήσας. 26.12 ∆ημιουργὸς καὶ βασιλεύς ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ. εἰμί. εἶπον γὰρ ὑμῖν ὡς «ἦν τις βασιλεὺς καὶ ἐπορεύθη ποιῆσαι γάμους τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ τῷ βασιλεῖ». 26.13 Ἄτρεπτός ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ. εἰμὶ καὶ ἐγώ. κεχρησμῴδηται γὰρ περὶ ἐμοῦ· «σὺ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σου οὐκ ἐκλείψουσιν». 26.14 Ἀπαθής ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ. εἰμί, ὡς καὶ τοὺς μετόχους μου ἀπαθείας μεταλαμβάνειν. 26.15 Ἄναρχος ὁ πατήρ. εἰμί. οὐ γὰρ ἦν ὅτε οὐκ εἶχεν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ τὸ ἐνυπόστατον ἀπαύγασμα καὶ τὸν «χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως» καὶ τὴν «εἰκόνα τῆς θεότητος», ἐμέ. 26.16 ζωὴ καὶ φῶς καὶ ἀγαθότης καὶ δύναμις καὶ σοφία καὶ ἀλήθεια καὶ ὅσα θεοῦ ἄξιά ἐστιν ὁ πατήρ. εἰμί, ὡς φθάσαντες ἠκούσατε. 26.17 Καὶ μέντοι καὶ σωτὴρ ἐγώ, «ἀνατέλλων τὸν ἥλιον ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ἁμαρτωλούς» καὶ οὐκ ἐπάγων «κακὸν ἀντὶ κακοῦ» 26.18 Φιλάνθρωπος ὁ πατήρ. εἰμί, ὅπουγε ὑμῶν ἕνεκα «ἐμαυτὸν ἐκένωσα μορφὴν δούλου λαβών», καὶ ῥαπιζόντων καὶ ἐμπτυόντων καὶ ἐμπαιζόντων καὶ σταυρούντων ὑμῶν ἠνεσχόμην. 26.19 Πάντα οὖν εἶπεν τὰ πατρικὰ τυγχάνειν αὐτοῦ, ὥστε μηδὲν πλέον διδόναι τῷ θεῷ πατρὶ ἢ μόνον τὸ εἶναι πατέρα υἱοῦ συνανάρχου καὶ συνυφεστῶτος 26.20 Οὕτω πιστεύειν ἀναπείθει καὶ τό· «πάντα τὰ ἐμὰ σά ἐστιν καὶ τὰ σὰ ἐμά, καὶ δεδόξασμαι ἐν αὐτοῖς». 26.21 εἰ γὰρ μὴ διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν σχέσιν ὧδε ἐλέχθη καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς πατρικοῖς οὐσιωδῶς δεδόξασται ὁ υἱός, εἰ μὴ βασιλεία καὶ δεσποτεία μία τυγχάνει, ἆρα, κατά γε λόγον αἱρετικόν, ἔστιν ἃ μὴ ὑπὸ τὴν τοῦ πατρός, ἀλλ' ὑπὸ τὴν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ υἱοῦ τελεῖ. 26.22 Καὶ πάλιν· «ἐὰν ἐγὼ δοξάζω ἐμαυτόν, ἡ δόξα μου οὐδέν ἐστιν· ἔστιν ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ δοξάζων με». 26.23 ἐμοί, φησίν, λέγοντι περὶ τῆς ἐμαυτοῦ θεϊκῆς δόξης, ὅτι «ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν», ἀπιστεῖτε· ἀλλ' ἔστιν ὁ μαρτυρῶν μοι πατήρ, ὅτι κατὰ φύσιν δοξάζομαι, υἱὸς μὲν ὢν αὐτοῦ ἀγαπητὸς καὶ ἀληθινός, θεὸς δὲ ὑμῶν καὶ δεσπότης. 26.24 Εἶτα λέγει· «πάτερ, δόξασόν σου τὸν υἱόν, ἵνα καὶ ὁ υἱός σου δοξάσῃ σε». ἴση κἀνταῦθα ἐφυλάχθη τιμή τε καὶ δόξα ταῖς θείαις ὑποστάσεσιν. ᾧ γὰρ ἂν ὑπολάβωμεν τρόπῳ τὸν πατέρα δοξάζειν τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ, τούτῳ αὐτὸς δοξάζεται ὑπ' αὐτοῦ. 26.25 Καὶ αὖθις ἐπάγει· «καὶ νῦν δόξασόν με, πάτερ, παρὰ σεαυτῷ τῇ δόξῃ, ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι παρὰ σοί». 26.26 φρικτὸν ἀκοῇ, ὅτι ὁ δόξαν ἔχων ἀνάρχως παρὰ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ πατρί–τοῦτο γὰρ σημαίνει τό· ᾖ εἶχον δόξῃ πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι–ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν οὐ δοξάζεται. 26.27 ποία δὲ ἦν αὕτη; ἣν ὡς οἶμαι καὶ 27 Μάρκος ἔφη· «ὅταν ἔλθῃ ὁ υἱὸς ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ», ἀντὶ τοῦ· τὴν πατρικὴν δόξαν ἔχει καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ ἥξει τὸ δεύτερον. 26.28 ὧν δὲ ἡ δόξα μία, οὐκ ἄλλη καὶ ἄλλη θεότης καὶ βασιλεία καὶ προσκύνησις καθέστηκεν. 26.29 ὅθεν προπαραγγέλλει «πιστεύετε εἰς τὸν θεὸν καὶ εἰς ἐμὲ πιστεύετε. ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ τοῦ πατρός μου μοναὶ πολλαί εἰσιν». 26.30 «τῆς γὰρ θεότητος», φησίν, «διαφορὰν οὐκ ἐχούσης, μίαν πίστεως γνῶσιν περὶ τῆς τριάδος ἔχειν ὀφείλετε, ἵν' οὕτω κατασκηνώσητε ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς τρισμακαρίσταις αὐλαῖς ταῖς πᾶσιν ἁρμοδίαις τε καὶ ἀρκούσαις». 26.31 Οὐ μόνον γοῦν τὰ ὑφηγητοῦ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ θεοῦ παρέχων λέγει· «ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι». προσέχεις κἀνταῦθα τὸ αὐτεξούσιον αὐτοῦ, ὅτι ὡσανεὶ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: ... that nothing acquired or worked by another is in himself, but from home] he brings in all the good things, showing [it], he gives according to authority the one divine peace, of which 'there is no boundary', about which Isaiah has cried out: 'Lord our God, give us peace; for you gave back to us all things. Lord, apart from you we know no other', as being his on account of the commonness of the nature and lordship. 26.3 For he said: 'peace I leave to you, my peace I give to you'. 26.4 Wherefore not least Paul too said that both the uncreated hypostases supply this God-given thing without variation, 26.5 having written to the Romans somewhere thus: 'grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ'. 26.6 And this also afforded us discernment that this very thing is so: 'all things whatever the Father has are mine'. 26.7 For these are taken, not ignorantly, not toward the creation, but toward the divine worth, if one must say 'worth' in the case of God. 26.8 For the Father, he says, is God. I am too; for [I am] his Son, only-begotten and true and beloved. 26.9 The Father is Lord. I too am Lord of all and heir of a living Father, being master of the inheritance. 26.10 And I inherit his things, on the one hand as their maker, on the other hand also as genuine Son. 26.11 But I was appointed heir as having become man. 26.12 The Father is Creator and King. I am. For I told you that 'there was a certain king and he went to make a wedding for his son the king'. 26.13 The Father is unchangeable. I am too. For it has been oracularly sung about me: 'you are the same, and your years will not fail'. 26.14 The Father is impassible. I am, so that those sharing in me also partake of impassibility. 26.15 The Father is without beginning. I am. For there was not when he did not have the name of the Father and the subsisting radiance of his glory and the 'imprint of the hypostasis' and the 'image of the Godhead', me. 26.16 Life and light and goodness and power and wisdom and truth and whatever things are worthy of God the Father is. I am, as you heard beforehand. 26.17 And indeed I too am Savior, 'making the sun rise upon righteous and sinners' and not bringing 'evil for evil'. 26.18 The Father is loving to mankind. I am, since for your sake 'I emptied myself, having taken the form of a slave', and I bore with you striking and spitting on and mocking and crucifying [me]. 26.19 So he said that all the Father's things happen to be his, so as to give nothing more to God the Father than only being Father of a Son co-without-beginning and co-subsisting. 26.20 This also persuades to believe so: 'all mine are yours and yours mine, and I have been glorified in them'. 26.21 For if it was not said thus on account of the natural relation and the Son has not been glorified essentially with all the Father's things, if kingdom and lordship does not happen to be one, then, according to heretical reasoning at least, there are things which are completed not under the [authority] of the Father, but under the authority of the Son. 26.22 And again: 'if I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me'. 26.23 To me, he says, saying about my own divine glory that 'I and the Father are one', you disbelieve; but there is the Father witnessing to me that I am glorified according to nature, being his Son, beloved and true, and your God and Master. 26.24 Then he says: 'Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you'. Equal honor and glory has here too been guarded for the divine hypostases. pass_b_english: … he brings in all good things. This he shows by giving, with authority, the one divine peace, of which “there is no end” (Isaiah 9:7), and of which Isaiah cried aloud: “O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us all things. O Lord, we know no other besides you” (Isaiah 26:12–13). He gives it as his own, because nature and lordship are held in common. For he said: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27).

That is why Paul too, and not least, said that both uncreated hypostases supply this God-given gift without any difference, writing to the Romans somewhere in these words: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7). And this saying too has given us to discern that the matter stands so: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). For no one who is not ignorant takes these words of the creation; they are taken of the divine rank, if one must speak of rank in the case of God.

“For the Father,” he says, “is God. So am I, for I am his only-begotten, true and beloved Son. The Father is Lord. I too am Lord of all, and heir of a living Father, master of the inheritance. I inherit what is his, partly as its maker and partly as his true-born Son; but I was appointed heir as one who became man. The Father is Creator and King. So am I, for I told you that ‘there was a certain king, and he went to make a wedding feast for his son the king’ (Matthew 22:2). The Father is unchangeable. So am I, for it has been prophesied of me: ‘You are the same, and your years will not fail’ (Psalm 102:27). The Father is impassible. So am I, so that those who share in me also partake of impassibility. The Father is without beginning. So am I. For there was never a time when he did not have the name of Father, and did not have me, the subsisting radiance of his glory, the ‘exact imprint of his hypostasis’ (Hebrews 1:3) and the ‘image of the Godhead.’ Life and light and goodness and power and wisdom and truth, and all that is worthy of God: this the Father is. So am I, as you have already heard. And indeed I too am Savior, ‘making the sun rise on the righteous and on sinners’ (Matthew 5:45), and not bringing ‘evil for evil.’ The Father loves mankind. So do I, since for your sake ‘I emptied myself, taking the form of a slave’ (Philippians 2:7), and bore with you as you struck me, spat on me, mocked me and crucified me.”

So he said that all the Father’s attributes are his, so as to grant God the Father nothing more than this alone: to be Father of a Son who is without beginning together with him and subsists together with him. This saying too persuades us to believe so: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them” (John 17:10). For if this was not said because of their natural relation, and if the Son has not been glorified in his essence with all that is the Father’s, if there is not one kingdom and one lordship, then, by heretical reasoning at least, there are things that fall not under the Father’s authority but under the Son’s.

And again: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me” (John 8:54). “When I speak to you,” he says, “of my own divine glory, that ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), you do not believe. But there is the Father who bears witness to me that I am glorified by nature, since I am his beloved and true Son, and your God and Master.” Then he says: “Father, glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you” (John 17:1). Here too equal honor and glory are kept for the divine hypostases. For in whatever way we take the Father to glorify his Son, in that same way he himself is glorified by him.

And again he goes on: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself with the glory that I had with you before the world was” (John 17:5). It is dreadful to hear: he who has glory without beginning with his own Father, for this is what “with the glory that I had before the world was” means, is not glorified by heretics. And what was this glory? The one that Mark too, I think, spoke of: “when the Son comes in the glory of his Father” (Mark 8:38), which is to say: he has the Father’s glory, and in it he will come the second time. And those whose glory is one do not have one Godhead, kingdom and worship here and another there. Hence he charges them beforehand: “Believe in God, and believe in me. In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:1–2). “For since the Godhead,” he says, “admits no difference, you must hold one knowledge of faith concerning the Trinity, so that in this way you may dwell in those thrice-blessed courts, which are fitting and sufficient for all.”
So, granting not only what a teacher grants but also what God grants, he says: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5:20). Here too you notice his sovereign freedom: that, as it were, …

choices.issue: Old draft garbled in many clauses, with invented sentences and missing references
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English broke the opening sentence and made 'all good things' be 'drawn toward' peace; called the hypostases 'unbegotten' (ἀγενήτους, uncreated) and the gift a 'God-giving word'; made the Son say 'he is his only-begotten' (26.8, 'I am'); rendered φθάσαντες ἠκούσατε 'as you have heard by those who have perished' (26.16, 'as you have already heard'); invented 'We were not misled' and 'in accordance with the Fathers' (26.19, τὰ πατρικά, the Father's attributes); gave συνανάρχου as 'co-ruling'; garbled 26.15, 26.21 ('it would be heretical'), 26.23, 26.26 ('independently from his own Father', 'according to the heretics'), 26.30 ('that they may know') and 26.31 ('those he led'). References: Isaiah 9:7 added for 'there is no end'; Isaiah 26:12 widened to 26:12-13; Hebrews 1:3 added; Luke 7:48 replaced by Luke 5:20, whose wording (σοι) Didymus quotes; four abbreviated references written out.

choices.why: Printed page number of the copy-text; skipped.

choices.term: δ' ἐπάγεσθαι τἀγαθὰ πάντα παριστῶν … δίδωσιν
choices.english: … he brings in all good things. This he shows by giving …
choices.why: The section opens inside a sentence begun in the previous section; παριστῶν governs the infinitives there and here, and δίδωσιν is the main verb. Only the words held here are translated, opening with an ellipsis.
Single-ν ἀγένητος means 'not come into being'; Didymus would not call the Son 'unbegotten' (ἀγέννητος).

choices.term: «κύριε ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν, εἰρήνην δὸς ἡμῖν … ἄλλον οὐκ οἴδαμεν»; «ὅριον οὐκ ἔστιν»
choices.why: Didymus quotes the Greek Isaiah, whose wording differs from the Hebrew-based English ('give us peace' for 'ordain peace'); the verse numbers are the same. 'Of his peace there is no end' is Greek Isaiah 9:6, English 9:7.
Greek Psalm 101:28, converted to English numbering and checked by verse text.

choices.term: ταῦτα γὰρ οὐκ ἀμαθῶς εἰς τὴν κτίσιν … ἐκλαμβάνεται
choices.english: For no one who is not ignorant takes these words of the creation
choices.why: οὐκ ἀμαθῶς qualifies the right reading: only ignorance would refer 'all that the Father has' to created things.

choices.term: εἰ ἀξίαν ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ φάναι χρή
choices.english: if one must speak of rank in the case of God

choices.term: Θεὸς γάρ, φησίν, ἐστὶν ὁ πατήρ … ἠνεσχόμην (26.8-26.18)
choices.english: set as the Son's speech in quotation marks
choices.why: φησίν makes the Son the speaker; Didymus voices him in the first person. Scripture inside the speech is set in single quotation marks.

choices.english: So am I / So do I
choices.why: The short reply after each title of the Father; 'So do I' after 'loves mankind' for English grammar.

choices.term: τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ … ἐμέ (26.15)
choices.english: the name of Father, and … me, the subsisting radiance of his glory
choices.why: εἶχεν governs both 'the name of Father' and ἐμέ, which stands in apposition to the radiance, the imprint and the image; see problems.
The radiance of Hebrews 1:3 as a real hypostasis, not a quality of the Father.

choices.english: without beginning together with him and subsists together with him
choices.why: Both compounds with συν- say the Son shares the Father's lack of beginning and his subsistence; 'co-ruling' (old draft) confused ἄναρχος with ἄρχω.
ὑπό with the genitive is the agent; the scandal is that heretics withhold the glory.
Self-determining power: he forgives on his own authority, as the next section goes on to say.
The sentence continues in the next section; only the words held here are translated.
